4 - linguistic typology.analytic language: a type of language that primarily relies on word order and function words to convey grammatical relationships, rather than inflections or word endings
4 - linguistic typology.morphological typology: a classification system used in linguistics to categorize languages based on their patterns of word formation and the ways in which they use affixes, inflections, and other morphological processes
4 - linguistic typology.agglutinative language: a type of language where words are formed by adding prefixes or suffixes to a base root, with each affix having a clear and consistent grammatical meaning
4 - linguistic typology.fusional language: a type of language where words undergo internal changes, such as vowel changes or consonant modifications, to indicate grammatical relationships, such as tense, number, and case
4 - linguistic typology.monosyllabic language: a type of language where the majority of words are composed of a single syllable
4 - linguistic typology.zero-marking language: a type of language in which grammatical relationships, such as tense, number, or case, are not explicitly indicated by the use of morphological markers or inflections
4 - linguistic typology.language family: a group of languages that are believed to have descended from a common ancestral language
4 - linguistic typology.cross-linguistic comparison: the process of analyzing and contrasting linguistic elements across different languages to identify similarities and differences
4 - linguistic typology.alignment: the systematic association or correspondence between linguistic units, such as sounds, words, or grammatical structures, within a language or across languages
4 - linguistic typology.ergative–absolutive alignment: a grammatical system where the subject of an intransitive verb (absolutive) is treated differently from the subject of a transitive verb (ergative), often found in languages that exhibit ergativity
4 - linguistic typology.nominative–accusative alignment: a grammatical system where the subject of an intransitive verb (nominative) is treated similarly to the subject of a transitive verb (nominative), while the object of a transitive verb (accusative) is marked differently, commonly found in languages that exhibit accusativity
4 - linguistic typology.active–stative alignment: a grammatical system where verbs in a language are marked or behave differently based on whether the subject is considered volitional or agentive (active) or non-volitional or experiencer-like (stative), often found in languages that exhibit such semantic distinctions
4 - linguistic typology.austronesian alignment: the typological pattern of grammatical alignment found in languages belonging to the austronesian language family
4 - linguistic typology.morphosyntactic alignment: the way in which grammatical markers and morphological processes interact with the syntax of a language to determine the alignment pattern between arguments and verb forms
4 - linguistic typology.tripartite alignment: a grammatical system in which the arguments of a verb are marked differently based on their grammatical role
4 - linguistic typology.split ergativity: a phenomenon in which a language exhibits a mixed pattern of ergative-absolutive alignment in some grammatical contexts and nominative-accusative alignment in others
4 - linguistic typology.nominative–absolutive alignment: a grammatical system where the subject of an intransitive verb (nominative) is treated similarly to the subject of a transitive verb (nominative), while the object of a transitive verb (absolutive) is marked differently
4 - linguistic typology.direct-inverse language: a type of grammatical system in which verbs are marked to indicate the semantic role relationships between the subject and object(s) of a sentence
4 - linguistic typology.secundative language: a type of language that exhibits a particular alignment pattern in the marking of the object of a transitive verb
4 - linguistic typology.dependent-marking language: a type of language where grammatical relationships between words are primarily marked on the dependent or non-head elements of a construction, rather than on the head or main element
4 - linguistic typology.head-marking language: a type of language where grammatical relationships between words are primarily marked on the head or main elements of a construction, rather than on the dependents
4 - linguistic typology.null-subject language: a type of language where the subject of a sentence can be omitted or left unexpressed when it can be inferred from the context
4 - linguistic typology.polysynthetic language: a type of language in which words are constructed by combining multiple morphemes to express complex meanings
4 - linguistic typology.ideophone: a type of word or linguistic form found in certain languages that vividly describes sensory perceptions or states, often related to sound, movement, color, or other sensory experiences

5 - morphology and lexicology.abbreviation: the shortened form of a word, etc.
5 - morphology and lexicology.affixation: a process in morphology where affixes, which are bound morphemes, are attached to a base or root morpheme to create new words or modify the meaning or grammatical function of existing words
5 - morphology and lexicology.affix: (grammar) a letter or group of letters added to the end or beginning of a word to change its meaning
5 - morphology and lexicology.contraction: a short form of a word or a group of words used instead of the full form
5 - morphology and lexicology.prefix: (grammar) a letter or a set of letters that are added to the beginning of a word to alter its meaning and make a new word
5 - morphology and lexicology.ending: the last part of a word, added to the main part
5 - morphology and lexicology.suffix: (grammar) a letter or a set of letters that are added to the end of a word to alter its meaning and make a new word
5 - morphology and lexicology.acronym: an abbreviation formed from the initial letters of a group of words, which can be pronounced as a word
5 - morphology and lexicology.blending: a process in language where two or more words are combined to create a new word that retains elements or sounds from the original words
5 - morphology and lexicology.neologism: the process of inventing a word
5 - morphology and lexicology.numeronym: a type of abbreviation in which a word or phrase is represented by a series of numbers, with the numbers typically corresponding to the number of letters omitted between the first and last letter of the word or phrase
5 - morphology and lexicology.bound morpheme: a morpheme that cannot stand alone as an independent word and must be attached to other morphemes to convey meaning
5 - morphology and lexicology.circumfix: a type of affix that consists of two parts, one attached to the beginning of a word and the other attached to the end
5 - morphology and lexicology.transfixation: a morphological process in which a segment or a group of segments is inserted within a word, typically resulting in a change of the word's meaning or grammatical category
5 - morphology and lexicology.analogy: (linguistics) a process by which a new word or inflection is formed according to existing rules and regulations
5 - morphology and lexicology.coinage: the process of inventing a word
5 - morphology and lexicology.stem: the core or base form of a word to which affixes (prefixes, suffixes, infixes, etc.) can be attached
5 - morphology and lexicology.root: the core lexical unit from which words are derived and carries the central meaning of a word
5 - morphology and lexicology.free morpheme: a morpheme that can function as an independent word in a language
5 - morphology and lexicology.infix: a type of bound morpheme that is inserted within a word, rather than being added as a prefix (before) or a suffix (after)
5 - morphology and lexicology.clitic: a linguistic element that functions as a word but behaves phonologically or syntactically as a bound morpheme, often attaching to other words and lacking independent stress or full syntactic independence
5 - morphology and lexicology.word formation: the process of creating new words or modifying existing ones through morphological and lexical mechanisms in a language
5 - morphology and lexicology.lexeme: (linguistics) a basic linguistic unit that is meaningful and underlies a set of words which are related through inflection
5 - morphology and lexicology.derivation: a morphological process in language where new words are formed by adding affixes or making internal modifications to a base or root word, resulting in a change in meaning, part of speech, or both
5 - morphology and lexicology.inflection: (grammar) a change in the structure of a word, usually adding a suffix, according to its grammatical function
5 - morphology and lexicology.back-formation: a word-formation process in which a new word is created by removing what is mistakenly perceived as a derivative affix from an existing word, often resulting in a shorter word with a different part of speech
5 - morphology and lexicology.compounding: a word-formation process in which two or more individual words are combined to create a new word, typically resulting in a compound with a meaning that is related to or derived from the meanings of the individual words
5 - morphology and lexicology.conversion: a word-formation process in which a word changes its grammatical category or part of speech without any accompanying morphological changes, such as when a noun becomes a verb or a verb becomes a noun
5 - morphology and lexicology.paradigm: a systematic arrangement of inflected forms or word forms that represent the different grammatical variations of a word or morpheme
5 - morphology and lexicology.lexicon: the complete set of meaningful units in a language or a branch of knowledge, or words or phrases that a speaker uses
5 - morphology and lexicology.clipping: a word-formation process in which a word is shortened by removing one or more syllables, usually from the beginning or end, resulting in a new word with the same or similar meaning as the original word
5 - morphology and lexicology.hypocorism: a word-formation process in which a word or name is modified to create a shorter, affectionate, or informal version, often used to express familiarity, endearment, or intimacy
5 - morphology and lexicology.morphemization: the process of creating or treating a group of phonological segments as a distinct morpheme, which carries meaning and can be combined with other morphemes to form words
5 - morphology and lexicology.agglutination: a morphological process in language where affixes are added to a root or base word in a clear, one-to-one fashion, each affix typically expressing a single grammatical or semantic meaning, resulting in a string of affixes attached to the root without any change in the affixes themselves
5 - morphology and lexicology.lexical morpheme: a type of morpheme that carries the core lexical or semantic meaning of a word
5 - morphology and lexicology.vocabulary: all the words used in a particular language or subject
5 - morphology and lexicology.derivative: (grammar) a word that is developed from another word or base
5 - morphology and lexicology.base: the form to which affixes or other morphological operations are added to create a new word
5 - morphology and lexicology.nominalization: a process in language where a word or phrase, typically a verb or an adjective, is transformed into a noun, either by adding a suffix or by changing its syntactic function, allowing the expression of concepts or actions as nominal entities
5 - morphology and lexicology.lexicalization: a process in which a word or phrase evolves from being a combination of grammatical elements or a non-lexicalized expression to becoming an established lexical unit with its own meaning and usage
5 - morphology and lexicology.diminutive: a word form or affix that is added to a base word to express smallness, endearment, or a sense of familiarity
5 - morphology and lexicology.protologism: a newly created word or expression that has not yet gained widespread acceptance or recognition within a language community
5 - morphology and lexicology.ghost word: a non-existent or erroneous word that has been mistakenly created and entered into a dictionary or other linguistic sources
5 - morphology and lexicology.pseudoword: a string of letters or sounds that resemble real words but do not have any actual meaning or lexical representation in a particular language
5 - morphology and lexicology.nonce word: a term or expression created and used for a specific occasion or context, typically with a limited or one-time purpose, and not intended for long-term or widespread usage
5 - morphology and lexicology.hapax legomenon: a word or form that appears only once within a specific corpus or body of text
5 - morphology and lexicology.morph: the smallest meaningful unit of language that carries a distinct semantic or grammatical function and cannot be further divided into smaller parts with independent meaning
5 - morphology and lexicology.morpheme: (linguistics) the smallest meaningful unit of a language that does not necessarily stand alone and cannot be divided
5 - morphology and lexicology.functional morpheme: a type of morpheme that conveys grammatical information and serves a functional role in a sentence, rather than carrying lexical or content-related meaning
5 - morphology and lexicology.lexical unit: (linguistics) a word, a group of words or a part of word that has a meaning and forms the basic element of any language
5 - morphology and lexicology.portmanteau word: a new word that is formed by the combination of two other words blending their meaning and sounds
5 - morphology and lexicology.lexis: (linguistics) all the words and phrases of a language, including the function words
5 - morphology and lexicology.word: (grammar) a unit of language that has a specific meaning
5 - morphology and lexicology.collocation: a particular combination of words that are used together very often
5 - morphology and lexicology.idiom: a group of words or a phrase that has a meaning different from the literal interpretation of its individual words, often specific to a particular language or culture
5 - morphology and lexicology.lexical ambiguity: a situation in which a word or phrase has multiple meanings or interpretations, often leading to confusion or uncertainty in understanding the intended message or context
5 - morphology and lexicology.reduplication: the process of repeating or duplicating all or part of a word or morpheme to create a new form, often with a change in meaning or grammatical function
5 - morphology and lexicology.blocking: a phenomenon where the presence of one linguistic form prevents the occurrence or acceptance of another form with a similar meaning or function
5 - morphology and lexicology.lexical rule: a set of principles or patterns that govern the formation or derivation of words and their meanings within a particular language or lexical system
5 - morphology and lexicology.sniglet: a playful, made-up word used to describe something for which there is no existing term, often adding humor and creativity to language
5 - morphology and lexicology.phono-semantic matching: the process in which a new word or morpheme is created by combining a sound component that resembles an existing word with a semantic component that reflects its meaning

6 - etymology and historical linguistics.etymon: the earliest known form of a word or a morpheme from which related words in different languages are derived
6 - etymology and historical linguistics.calque: (linguistics) a loan word or expression that is a word-by-word translation of a word or expression in another language
6 - etymology and historical linguistics.loanword: a word or phrase borrowed from one language and incorporated into another language, typically with some modifications to fit the phonological, morphological, and/or semantic patterns of the borrowing language
6 - etymology and historical linguistics.borrowing: the process by which words or phrases are adopted from one language into another, often due to cultural contact, trade, or historical influences, resulting in the integration of foreign elements into the borrowing language
6 - etymology and historical linguistics.origin: the source or point of beginning of something, such as the historical, cultural, or linguistic roots of a word, concept, or phenomenon
6 - etymology and historical linguistics.cognate word: a word that shares a common origin with another word in a different language, usually demonstrating similarities in form and meaning due to their common ancestral language
6 - etymology and historical linguistics.false etymology: the incorrect or mistaken explanation of the origin and development of a word or phrase based on popular belief or folk etymological reasoning
6 - etymology and historical linguistics.folk etymology: the process by which the form or meaning of a word is modified or reinterpreted based on the similarity or familiarity of its components to other words or familiar patterns, often resulting in a new, popular, but etymologically incorrect explanation
6 - etymology and historical linguistics.morphological leveling: a process in language change where irregularities in the inflectional or derivational morphology of words are simplified or regularized over time
6 - etymology and historical linguistics.morphological erosion: the process by which the complexity or number of morphological elements in a word or word form is reduced over time
6 - etymology and historical linguistics.phonetic erosion: the gradual simplification or loss of certain sounds or phonetic features within a language over time
6 - etymology and historical linguistics.semantic erosion: the process whereby the original meaning or intensity of a word or expression becomes progressively weakened or diluted over time, resulting in a broader, less specific, or less potent semantic range
6 - etymology and historical linguistics.de-categorialization: the process by which a word or morpheme loses its original grammatical category and acquires a more independent, lexical function
6 - etymology and historical linguistics.language change: the natural and ongoing process by which languages evolve and transform over time
6 - etymology and historical linguistics.lexical change: the process of modification and evolution in the vocabulary of a language over time
6 - etymology and historical linguistics.internal reconstruction: a method used in historical linguistics to infer and reconstruct the linguistic forms and features of an earlier stage of a language based on evidence from its present-day descendants
6 - etymology and historical linguistics.language contact: the interaction of speakers from different linguistic backgrounds, leading to the exchange and influence of linguistic features between languages
6 - etymology and historical linguistics.grammaticalization: a process in language change whereby words or lexical items evolve over time to become grammatical markers or functional elements, often losing their original lexical meaning and acquiring grammatical or structural functions
6 - etymology and historical linguistics.grimm's law: a fundamental principle in historical linguistics that describes the systematic sound changes observed in the transition from proto-indo-european to germanic languages, including the transformation of certain consonant sounds
6 - etymology and historical linguistics.substrate language: a language that has lower prestige or social power in a contact situation and influences another language (superstrate) with which it comes into contact, leaving a significant impact on its linguistic features, vocabulary, and structure
6 - etymology and historical linguistics.semantic shift: the phenomenon in which the meaning of a word or expression changes over time, resulting in a different interpretation or connotation from its original usage
6 - etymology and historical linguistics.diachronic analysis: the study and examination of language change and evolution over time, focusing on the historical development of linguistic features, structures, and patterns in a language or language family
6 - etymology and historical linguistics.synchronic analysis: the examination and study of a language at a specific point in time, emphasizing its existing linguistic features, structures, and patterns without considering their historical development or changes over time
6 - etymology and historical linguistics.comparative method: a linguistic approach that compares related languages to uncover their shared ancestral forms and relationships
6 - etymology and historical linguistics.swadesh list: a standardized set of basic vocabulary words used in comparative linguistics to analyze similarities and differences between languages, typically consisting of around 100 to 200 words that are considered to be less subject to borrowing or change over time
6 - etymology and historical linguistics.derivation: the process of creating new words over time through linguistic changes and transformations
6 - etymology and historical linguistics.centum language: a classification of indo-european languages in which the palatal or velar stops of the proto-indo-european language merged with the plain stops, resulting in a lack of a phonemic distinction between them
6 - etymology and historical linguistics.satem language: a type of indo-european language in which the original palatal or velar consonants evolved into fricatives or affricates, distinguishing it from centum languages that preserved these consonants as stops
6 - etymology and historical linguistics.suppletion: the phenomenon in which an irregular form of a word, often a verb or adjective, is used instead of a regular form to express a different grammatical feature
6 - etymology and historical linguistics.semantic narrowing: a process in language change where the meaning of a word becomes more specific or limited over time, often referring to a narrower subset of the original meaning
6 - etymology and historical linguistics.internal linguistic change: changes that occur within a language over time without the influence of external factors
6 - etymology and historical linguistics.language cluster: a group of languages that are genetically related and share common features, indicating a common origin or ancestry

7 - semantics.synonymy: the relationship between words or expressions that have similar or identical meanings, or nearly identical meanings, in a particular context or language
7 - semantics.antonymy: the relationship between words or expressions that have opposite or contrasting meanings
7 - semantics.hyponymy: a hierarchical relationship between words, where one word (the hyponym) represents a more specific or subordinate category within the meaning of another word (the hypernym)
7 - semantics.prototype: an exemplary representation of a category that embodies its essential features and serves as a reference for evaluating other members of the category
7 - semantics.homonymy: a linguistic phenomenon where words share the same form (spelling or pronunciation) but have different meanings, contributing to lexical ambiguity and requiring context for proper interpretation
7 - semantics.homophony: a linguistic phenomenon where different words have the same or similar pronunciation but may have different spellings and meanings, resulting in potential confusion and ambiguity in oral communication
7 - semantics.polysemy: the phenomenon in language where a single word has multiple related meanings or senses, allowing for flexibility and richness of expression through context-dependent interpretation
7 - semantics.catachresis: a type of figurative language that involves the unconventional or strained use of words, often resulting in an unexpected or exaggerated expression
7 - semantics.scope: the extent or range of meaning that a word, phrase, or grammatical construction has within a sentence or discourse
7 - semantics.modality: the way in which language expresses the speaker's or writer's attitude, opinion, or degree of certainty regarding a statement or proposition
7 - semantics.semantic network: a graphical representation or structure that depicts relationships between concepts or entities in a language or knowledge domain
7 - semantics.word sense: the specific meaning or interpretation of a word in a given context or language
7 - semantics.troponymy: the study of how one word's meaning represents a specific way or type of another word's meaning within a particular category or field of language
7 - semantics.thematic role: a grammatical concept that represents the relationship between a noun phrase and the action or state described by a verb, indicating the role or function of the noun phrase in the event or situation
7 - semantics.semantic satiation: a psychological phenomenon where repeated exposure to a word or phrase leads to a temporary loss of its meaning or sense of familiarity
7 - semantics.lexical chain: a sequence of words or terms in a text that are semantically related or connected by their meaning
7 - semantics.semantic field: a group or set of words that are related in meaning and share a common semantic theme or category
7 - semantics.semantic relation: the connections or associations between words or concepts based on their meaning
7 - semantics.conceptual metaphor: a cognitive mechanism in which abstract or complex ideas are understood and expressed in terms of more concrete or familiar concepts
7 - semantics.conceptual metonymy: a cognitive process in which one concept is understood or represented in terms of another concept based on a conceptual or cognitive association between them, often involving contiguity or a part-whole relationship
7 - semantics.agent: a grammatical role or semantic role that refers to the entity that performs or initiates an action or event in a sentence or a clause
7 - semantics.broadening: a process where the meaning of a word or concept expands or becomes more inclusive, encompassing a wider range of referents or interpretations than its original or core meaning
7 - semantics.epithet: a word or phrase applied to something to convey its character or essence in a descriptive sense
7 - semantics.word meaning: the specific sense or interpretation attributed to a word in a particular context
7 - semantics.accidental gap: a situation where a language lacks a specific word or lexical item to express a particular concept or meaning
7 - semantics.content word: a word that carries semantic meaning and contributes to the overall content and understanding of a sentence, such as nouns, verbs, adjectives, and adverbs
7 - semantics.concept: a principle or idea that is abstract
7 - semantics.meronymy: a linguistic concept that describes the relationship between a word that represents a whole object and a word that represents a part or subset of that object
7 - semantics.sign system: a structured system of signs, symbols, or codes that are used to communicate meaning within a particular context or domain
7 - semantics.circular definition: a type of definition that uses the term being defined as part of the definition itself, resulting in an uninformative or logically flawed explanation
7 - semantics.definition: the act or process of explaining the meaning of a word, concept, or term
7 - semantics.holonym: a term used in semantics and linguistics to refer to a word that represents a whole or complete entity, while its parts are referred to as meronyms.
7 - semantics.homograph: (grammar) one of two or more words that are spelled the same but differ in meaning
7 - semantics.descriptor: a word or phrase that describes or provides information about something
7 - semantics.denotation: the objective and dictionary-based meaning of a word, representing its core and universally accepted definition

15 - phonology.syllable-timed language: a type of language where each syllable is given roughly equal time and stress, resulting in a more evenly paced and rhythmic pattern of speech
15 - phonology.lenition: a phonological process where a consonant becomes weaker or less prominent in terms of articulation, often resulting in its softening, reduction, or loss of certain features
15 - phonology.rendaku: a phonological phenomenon in japanese where the initial consonant of the second element in a compound word undergoes voicing or consonant softening
15 - phonology.sandhi: the phonological process in which the pronunciation of sounds changes when they occur in specific phonetic contexts or in continuous speech
15 - phonology.consonant gradation: a phonological process where a consonant undergoes systematic changes in its articulation or voicing depending on its position within a word or in certain morphological contexts
15 - phonology.vowel harmony: a phonological process in which vowels within a word or across adjacent words become more similar or assimilate to each other in terms of certain phonetic features, typically involving vowel height, backness, or rounding
15 - phonology.tone sandhi: the phonological phenomenon where the tone of a word or syllable changes based on its position or interaction with neighboring tones, typically occurring in tonal languages
15 - phonology.tonal language: a language in which variations in pitch or tone can distinguish different words or convey different meanings
15 - phonology.imbrication: a phonological process in which adjacent or alternating segments in a word share a common feature, resulting in the assimilation or co-occurrence of certain articulatory or acoustic characteristics
15 - phonology.syncope: (phonetics) the omission or loss of one or more sounds from the pronunciation of a word
15 - phonology.digraph: two successive letters (especially two letters used to represent a single sound: `sh' in `shoe')
15 - phonology.nasalization: the process of producing a sound with nasal resonance, where air flows through the nasal cavity while a sound is being articulated
15 - phonology.insertion: the process of adding sounds, typically vowels or consonants, into a word or morpheme that are not present in its underlying or base form
15 - phonology.prothesis: a phonological process in which a sound or phoneme is added at the beginning of a word, typically to facilitate pronunciation or conform to phonotactic constraints
15 - phonology.terminal devoicing: a phonological process in which voiced consonants at the end of a word are pronounced as voiceless
15 - phonology.ablaut: a phonological phenomenon where a vowel in a word changes systematically to indicate grammatical or derivational distinctions, often resulting in different word forms or meanings
15 - phonology.regressive assimilation: a phonological process in which a sound is modified or assimilated to match a neighboring sound that comes after it
15 - phonology.haplology: a phonological process in which a repeated or similar sequence of sounds within a word or phrase is simplified or deleted, resulting in the loss of one of the similar elements
15 - phonology.intervocalic voicing: a phonological process in which a voiceless consonant between two vowels becomes voiced, typically due to the influence of the surrounding vowel sounds
15 - phonology.vowel reduction: the process in which a vowel in an unstressed position or in a particular phonological context becomes centralized and/or weakened, resulting in a reduced vowel quality
15 - phonology.palatalization: a phonological process in which a sound, typically a consonant, becomes palatal or acquires palatal characteristics under the influence of a neighboring palatal sound or due to the position within a particular linguistic environment
15 - phonology.vrddhi: a phonological process in sanskrit and other indo-aryan languages where a vowel lengthens or becomes long as a result of specific phonetic and phonological conditions, often related to the presence of certain consonants or morphological factors
15 - phonology.crasis: the linguistic phenomenon where two or more adjacent words merge together, typically resulting in the contraction or fusion of sounds or syllables
15 - phonology.zero consonant: a phonological phenomenon where a consonant sound is not pronounced in a particular position within a word or a specific language context, often resulting in a phonetic gap or absence of sound
15 - phonology.allomorph: any of the variant forms of a morpheme, which are phonetically or phonologically conditioned
15 - phonology.sound symbolism: the phenomenon where certain sounds or phonetic patterns are associated with specific meanings or qualities, often independent of linguistic convention or arbitrary assignment
15 - phonology.mora: a unit of phonological timing that determines the length or duration of a syllable or a vowel sound
15 - phonology.null allomorph: a silent or phonetically empty form of a morpheme that represents its absence in certain linguistic environments
15 - phonology.cluster reduction: a phonological process in which one or more consonants in a consonant cluster are omitted or simplified in pronunciation
15 - phonology.rhotacism: a phonological process or phenomenon where a non-"r" sound is changed or replaced by an "r" sound, commonly observed in language evolution or dialectal variations
15 - phonology.palindrome: a word or phrase or sentence that is read the same backward as forward
15 - phonology.onomatopoeia: the naming of a thing or action based on the sound that they refer to
15 - phonology.phonestheme: a recurring sound pattern or sequence of phonemes that is associated with a particular meaning or connotation in language

16 - writing systems.script: a particular system or style of writing that uses specific symbols, characters, or graphical elements to represent language
16 - writing systems.defective script: a writing system that has significant limitations or deficiencies in representing the sounds, grammar, or vocabulary of a language, often leading to ambiguities, inconsistencies, or difficulties in accurately conveying meaning through writing
16 - writing systems.phonographic writing: a system of writing in which the written symbols or characters represent specific sounds or phonetic elements of a language, allowing for a more direct phonetic representation of words and language sounds
16 - writing systems.syllabary: a writing system in which each character represents a syllable, typically consisting of a consonant-vowel combination, allowing for the representation of a wide range of words and sounds within a language
16 - writing systems.cuneiform: one of the earliest known writing systems in human history, characterized by wedge-shaped marks or symbols impressed on clay tablets using a stylus
16 - writing systems.linear a: an undeciphered writing system used in the ancient aegean, particularly on the island of crete, during the bronze age
16 - writing systems.linear b: an ancient script used to write mycenaean greek during the late bronze age, featuring linear symbols representing syllables
16 - writing systems.semi-syllabary: a writing system that combines elements of both syllabaries and alphabets, where some symbols represent syllables while others represent individual consonant or vowel sounds
16 - writing systems.braille: a tactile writing system designed for individuals who are blind or visually impaired, utilizing patterns of raised dots that can be felt with the fingertips to represent letters, numbers, and other symbols
16 - writing systems.abjad: a type of writing system where only the consonantal sounds are represented, typically used in languages that rely heavily on consonants and have a limited number of vowel sounds
16 - writing systems.devanagari: an abugida script used for writing several languages in the indian subcontinent, known for its connected letterforms and versatile consonant-vowel combinations
16 - writing systems.abugida: a writing system in which each character represents a consonant-vowel combination, and the vowels are typically indicated by diacritic marks or modifications of the consonant symbol
16 - writing systems.hanzi script: a logographic writing system used for writing the chinese language, consisting of characters that represent morphemes or words and are composed of various strokes arranged in a square or rectangular shape
16 - writing systems.hieroglyph: a system of writing used in ancient egypt, consisting of pictorial symbols or characters that represent objects, ideas, or sounds, and were commonly used for inscriptions on temple walls, tombs, and other monumental structures
16 - writing systems.latin alphabet: the most widely used writing system in the world today, consisting of 26 letters and used to write numerous languages, including english, spanish, french, and many others
16 - writing systems.hangul: the native phonetic script of the korean language, created in the 15th century under the reign of king sejong the great
16 - writing systems.pinyin: a romanization system used for writing the pronunciation of chinese characters using the latin alphabet
16 - writing systems.aramaic alphabet: the writing system used to write the aramaic language, which has been historically significant in the middle east and has influenced several other scripts, including hebrew and arabic
16 - writing systems.hebrew alphabet: a writing system used for the hebrew language and other jewish languages, consisting of 22 consonant letters and a system of vowel markers
16 - writing systems.greek alphabet: an ancient writing system that has been used for over two thousand years, known for its distinctive letters and its significant influence on western alphabets
16 - writing systems.featural writing system: a type of writing system that represents phonetic features or articulatory gestures rather than individual sounds or symbols
16 - writing systems.cyrillic alphabet: an alphabet used to write various languages, including russian, ukrainian, bulgarian, and serbian, among others, and is named after the 9th-century byzantine scholar cyril, who was instrumental in its development
16 - writing systems.armenian alphabet: a distinct writing system developed in the 5th century ad to write the armenian language, featuring unique letter shapes and phonetic values
16 - writing systems.georgian alphabet: a unique writing system consisting of 33 letters and is used to write the georgian language, known for its distinct letter shapes and phonetic representation

17 - orthography and typography.spelling: the act or the ability of putting letters in the correct order to form a word
17 - orthography and typography.capitalization: the practice of using uppercase letters to signify the beginning of a sentence, proper nouns, and certain other grammatical elements for clarity and emphasis
17 - orthography and typography.punctuation: the use of marks such as a period, comma, etc. in writing to divide sentences and phrases to better convey meaning
17 - orthography and typography.writing system: a set of symbols or characters used to represent language in a visual or tangible form, allowing communication and the recording of information
17 - orthography and typography.phonemic orthography: a writing system that represents the sounds of a language using consistent and predictable symbols or characters, allowing for a direct correspondence between written and spoken forms
17 - orthography and typography.cursive: a style of handwriting in which the letters are joined together in a flowing manner, often written with continuous strokes and without lifting the pen or pencil from the paper
17 - orthography and typography.typography: the art and technique of arranging and organizing written text in a visually appealing and readable manner
17 - orthography and typography.paragraph: a self-contained part of discourse that consists of one or more sentences dealing with a particular topic, indicated by indentation
17 - orthography and typography.orthographic depth: the degree of consistency between the spelling and pronunciation of words in a writing system, with shallow orthographies having a high degree of consistency such as in spanish and deep orthographies having a lower consistency such as in english
17 - orthography and typography.lowercase: the small letters in a writing system, contrasting with uppercase, and is commonly used in regular text
17 - orthography and typography.uppercase: the set of capital or large letters in the latin alphabet or other writing systems, typically used at the beginning of a sentence, for proper nouns, and for emphasis
17 - orthography and typography.rebus principle: a linguistic or writing technique that uses pictures, symbols, or combinations of letters to represent words or sounds, often based on their phonetic similarity or association, creating visual puns or wordplay
17 - orthography and typography.alphabet: a set of basic written symbols, representing the sounds of a language, which if put into correct orders form the words
17 - orthography and typography.logogram: a written character or symbol that represents an entire word or concept, rather than representing individual sounds or phonetic elements, as seen in some writing systems such as chinese characters or egyptian hieroglyphs
17 - orthography and typography.serif: the small decorative strokes or flourishes that extend from the ends of the main strokes of letters in a typeface, giving them a more traditional or formal appearance
17 - orthography and typography.typeface: a particular design or style of lettering, including the shape, size, and characteristics of the characters, that make up a complete set of fonts within a specific font family
17 - orthography and typography.allograph: a different physical or visual representation of the same grapheme or character in a writing system
17 - orthography and typography.grapheme: the smallest unit of a writing system that represents a distinct sound or phoneme in a language, such as a single letter, combination of letters, or symbol
17 - orthography and typography.bold: a typographic style that emphasizes or highlights text by making it thicker and darker in appearance compared to the surrounding text
17 - orthography and typography.italic: a cursive script with slanted letters that are connected and flowing in appearance
17 - orthography and typography.sans serif: a typeface or font that does not have small decorative strokes or serifs at the ends of the main letterforms, giving it a clean and modern appearance
17 - orthography and typography.slashed zero: the typographic variation of the digit "0" in which a diagonal slash is added across the zero to distinguish it from the letter "o" and indicate that it represents the numerical zero
17 - orthography and typography.ligature: a typographic term that refers to the combination of two or more letters or characters into a single interconnected glyph, often used to enhance readability or aesthetic appeal in certain typefaces or scripts
17 - orthography and typography.diacritic: (linguistics) a mark that is written below or above a letter indicating a difference in pronunciation
17 - orthography and typography.acute accent: a diacritic used in various languages and writing systems to indicate different linguistic features such as stress, pitch, or vowel quality
17 - orthography and typography.accent: a mark that indicates the emphatic syllable in a word, which is stressed
17 - orthography and typography.tilde: the symbol ~ put over the letter n in spanish, or a and o in portuguese to indicate nasalization
17 - orthography and typography.cedilla: the mark , , put under the letter 'c' indicating that it has a /s/ sound, rather than a /k/ sound
17 - orthography and typography.circumflex: the mark ^, placed over a vowel in some languages indicating contraction, length, etc.
17 - orthography and typography.grave: the diacritic mark ` placed above a vowel in some languages indicating an altered pronunciation in case of quality, quantity or pitch
17 - orthography and typography.umlaut: the mark ¨, put over a vowel indicating an articulation with rounding or fronting
17 - orthography and typography.thorn: a letter in some historical germanic languages, such as old english and old norse, representing the "th" sound, and is characterized by its distinct angular shape resembling a "p" with a vertical stroke
17 - orthography and typography.pictograph: a graphic symbol that signifies a word, phrase, physical object, etc.
17 - orthography and typography.ideogram: a symbol or graphic representation that directly represents a concept or idea, often without relying on specific sounds or language, commonly used in pictographic or logographic writing systems
17 - orthography and typography.silent letter: a letter in a word that is not pronounced when the word is spoken, although it may still affect the pronunciation or meaning of the word
17 - orthography and typography.eth: a letter used in some languages, such as old english and icelandic, to represent the voiced "th" sound, and is derived from the runic letter "d"
17 - orthography and typography.virama: a diacritic mark used in some writing systems, such as devanagari and indic scripts, to indicate the absence of a vowel sound following a consonant, effectively suppressing the inherent vowel
17 - orthography and typography.calligraphy: the art of producing beautiful handwriting using special writing instruments such as a dip or brush pen
17 - orthography and typography.clerical script: a style of chinese calligraphy that emerged during the han dynasty and was commonly used for official documents and bureaucratic purposes, characterized by its simplified and standardized form with square-shaped characters and clear strokes
17 - orthography and typography.seal script: an ancient style of writing used in china during the late zhou dynasty and the qin dynasty, characterized by its pictographic and abstract forms, with characters often featuring intricate and flowing lines
17 - orthography and typography.regular script: a standardized style of chinese calligraphy characterized by its balanced and uniform strokes, widely used for its readability and simplicity
17 - orthography and typography.running hand script: a semi-cursive style of chinese calligraphy that exhibits a fluid and connected writing with simplified strokes, striking a balance between the cursive and regular scripts
17 - orthography and typography.kanji: the logographic characters adopted from chinese characters and used in the japanese writing system
17 - orthography and typography.hiragana: a fundamental component of the japanese writing system, comprising 46 characters that represent syllables and are utilized for native japanese words, grammatical purposes, and verb endings
17 - orthography and typography.katakana: a component in the japanese writing system, consisting of 46 characters that represent syllables and are primarily used for borrowed words, foreign names, onomatopoeia, and emphasis
17 - orthography and typography.hanja: the chinese characters that are used in the korean writing system, representing both meaning and sound and used in conjunction with the korean alphabet, hangul, to write words of chinese origin or to clarify the meaning of korean words
17 - orthography and typography.rune: a letter or character from the runic alphabet, used in various germanic languages during the early middle ages
17 - orthography and typography.stroke: a single mark or brush movement used to construct characters in writing systems like chinese, japanese, or korean

18 - punctuation.ampersand: the symbol & used in writing to signify the word 'and'
18 - punctuation.apostrophe: the symbol ' used in writing to show possession or omission of letters or numbers
18 - punctuation.asterisk: the symbol * used in writing or printing to show that there is more information about something in the footnote or as an indication of importance or omission
18 - punctuation.backslash: the symbol (\), used in some computer commands
18 - punctuation.brace: either of the two symbols { } used especially in mathematics or computing to show that the items within are connected together
18 - punctuation.bracket: each of the two symbols [ ] used to indicate that the enclosed numbers or words should be considered separately
18 - punctuation.bullet point: any of the various items in a list that are marked by a circle, square, diamond, etc. to indicate importance; the printed symbol is also called a bullet point
18 - punctuation.colon: the punctuation mark : used to introduce a quotation, explanation, or list of items
18 - punctuation.comma: the mark , used to separate items in a list or indicate a pause in a sentence
18 - punctuation.dash: the punctuation mark - used in writing to separate parts of a sentence, instead of a colon or brackets
18 - punctuation.ditto: the symbol〃used under a word in a list to show that it is repeated and to avoid writing it down again
18 - punctuation.dot: a small, round mark or spot
18 - punctuation.hyphen: the punctuation mark - used to join two words to form a new one, or to indicate an element is missing (as for instance right- and left-handed), or to show that the remaining letters of a word situated at the end of a line are at the beginning of the next one
18 - punctuation.mark: a symbol used in writing or in print that signifies or is a record of something
18 - punctuation.period: the symbol . used to mark the end of a sentence or an abbreviation
18 - punctuation.parenthesis: either of the symbols ( ) used in writing to enclose extra information that is given or to group a symbolic unit in logic or mathematics
18 - punctuation.point: the punctuation mark . used to indicate that a sentence or an abbreviation is ended
18 - punctuation.pound sign: the symbol £ used in writing or printing to represent the british unit of currency
18 - punctuation.punctuation mark: any mark such as a period, comma, brackets, etc., used in writing to divide phrases and sentences and to make them clearly understood
18 - punctuation.question mark: the mark ? used at the end of a sentence to show that it is a question
18 - punctuation.quotation mark: either of the symbols " " or ' ' used before and after a word or words to indicate the beginning and the end of a title or quoted remark, or to mark a jargon
18 - punctuation.quote: (plural) another way of saying quotation marks
18 - punctuation.semicolon: the punctuation mark ; used to separate the items in a list or to indicate a pause between two main clauses in a compound sentence
18 - punctuation.slash: the symbol / used in print or writing to indicate alternatives or fractions, etc.
18 - punctuation.hyphenation: the insertion of a hyphen (-) between syllables or parts of a word that cannot fit on a single line
18 - punctuation.double dagger: a punctuation symbol used to indicate additional information or a footnote reference in written text
18 - punctuation.bullet operator: a typographical symbol used to denote individual items in a list or to visually separate and organize information in a concise manner
18 - punctuation.section sign: a typographical symbol used to indicate a specific section or division within a document, often used in legal or academic contexts to reference a particular part or topic
18 - punctuation.guillemet: a single typographical symbol, either the opening or closing angle quotation mark (« or ») used in various languages to indicate quotations or enclose text with a special meaning
18 - punctuation.ampersat: the symbol @, that is used in email addresses and other forms of electronic communication
18 - punctuation.caret symbol: a small, v-shaped symbol often used in mathematics and computer programming to indicate exponentiation, bitwise xor operations, or to mark insertions or corrections in text
18 - punctuation.interpunct: a punctuation mark that consists of a small dot used to separate or clarify elements within a sentence, such as in decimal numbers, abbreviations, or to indicate word boundaries in some languages
18 - punctuation.ellipsis: a punctuation mark consisting of three dots that indicates the omission of words or a pause in speech, often used to create suspense, indicate trailing off, or show incomplete thoughts in writing
18 - punctuation.emoticon: a sign formed by keyboard characters to show the tone of a message or its sender's facial expression, used on social media or in text messages
18 - punctuation.interrobang: a punctuation mark that combines the question mark and exclamation mark, used to express a mixture of surprise and inquiry, or to convey a rhetorical question with emphasis
18 - punctuation.en dash: a punctuation mark that is slightly longer than a hyphen (-) and is used to indicate a range or connection between two elements, such as dates, times, or numbers. it can also be used to show contrast or connection between words or phrases
18 - punctuation.em dash: a punctuation mark that is longer than both a hyphen (-) and an en dash (–)
18 - punctuation.parenthetical comma: a punctuation mark used to set off nonessential or supplementary information within a sentence, indicating a slight pause or separation of the parenthetical element from the rest of the sentence
18 - punctuation.serial comma: a comma used before the conjunction (usually "and" or "or") in a list of three or more items, providing clarity and avoiding ambiguity
18 - punctuation.double quotation mark: a punctuation mark consisting of two parallel horizontal lines used to enclose quoted or cited material
18 - punctuation.single quotation mark: a punctuation mark consisting of a curved or slanted line used to enclose quoted or cited material within a larger quotation or to indicate a word or phrase as being ironic, unconventional, or used in a specialized sense
18 - punctuation.dagger: a typographical symbol resembling a cross or plus sign (+) that is often used to indicate a footnote or reference in written or printed text
18 - punctuation.exclamation point: the mark ! used after a sentence to indicate excitement, surprise, etc.
18 - punctuation.pilcrow: a typographical symbol that resembles a backward-facing "p" (¶)

19 - pragmatics and discourse analysis.linguistic context: the surrounding linguistic elements that contribute to the interpretation and meaning of a specific expression or utterance
19 - pragmatics and discourse analysis.deixis: the phenomenon in language where the interpretation of certain words or expressions depends on the context of the speaker, listener, and the surrounding situation
19 - pragmatics and discourse analysis.person deixis: a type of deixis that involves the use of pronouns and verb forms to refer to the participants in a conversation
19 - pragmatics and discourse analysis.spatial deixis: a type of deixis that involves the use of language to refer to spatial locations, such as indicating the direction, distance, or proximity of objects or places in relation to the speaker or the context of the conversation
19 - pragmatics and discourse analysis.temporal deixis: a type of deixis that involves the use of language to refer to specific points in time, such as indicating the past, present, or future, or expressing temporal relations and sequencing of events
19 - pragmatics and discourse analysis.direct speech: the representation of someone's words using quotation marks, presenting their exact utterances as they were spoken or written
19 - pragmatics and discourse analysis.indirect speech: the representation of someone's words by reporting or paraphrasing their statements without using direct quotation marks
19 - pragmatics and discourse analysis.speech act: an utterance or expression that not only conveys meaning but also performs a particular function or action in communication, such as making a request, giving an order, or making a promise
19 - pragmatics and discourse analysis.reference: the act of referring to or indicating something or someone in language, where words or expressions are used to point to or denote specific entities, objects, or concepts
19 - pragmatics and discourse analysis.face-threatening act: a communicative behavior or action that poses a risk to someone's positive face, their desired self-image or social identity, potentially leading to face loss or face-threatening situations.
19 - pragmatics and discourse analysis.face-saving act: a communicative behavior or action that helps to protect or restore someone's positive face, their desired self-image or social identity, in order to avoid or mitigate face loss or face-threatening situations
19 - pragmatics and discourse analysis.expression: a word or phrase, often an idiomatic one
19 - pragmatics and discourse analysis.caregiver speech: a speech style characterized by simplified language, exaggerated prosody, repetition, and high pitch, commonly used by caregivers when interacting with infants and young children
19 - pragmatics and discourse analysis.connected speech: the natural flow of spoken language where words and sounds are connected together, often resulting in changes in pronunciation, elision of sounds, and modifications in speech patterns
19 - pragmatics and discourse analysis.discourse marker: a linguistic element or phrase used in speech or writing to indicate the structure, organization, or relationship between different parts of a discourse, often serving to facilitate communication and signal the speaker's intentions or attitudes
19 - pragmatics and discourse analysis.framing: the cognitive and linguistic process of shaping and presenting information in a particular way to influence how people perceive and interpret it
19 - pragmatics and discourse analysis.dialogue: a conversation or exchange of ideas between two or more individuals, typically characterized by turn-taking, interactive communication, and mutual understanding
19 - pragmatics and discourse analysis.discourse: the use of language in a larger context, including conversations, written texts, and social interactions, where meaning is constructed and communicated through the organization and flow of language
19 - pragmatics and discourse analysis.intertextuality: the interconnectedness and referencing of texts, where one text refers to or influences another, creating layers of meaning and a complex web of relationships between texts
19 - pragmatics and discourse analysis.text: anything that is in written form
19 - pragmatics and discourse analysis.pejorative: language, words, or expressions that convey a negative or derogatory connotation and are intended to belittle, criticize, or insult someone or something
19 - pragmatics and discourse analysis.turn-taking: the process by which participants in a conversation alternate speaking and listening, following certain rules and cues to facilitate smooth and coherent communication
19 - pragmatics and discourse analysis.hedge: a linguistic device used to express uncertainty or vagueness, often through words or phrases that indicate a lack of commitment or certainty in one's statement
19 - pragmatics and discourse analysis.implicature: the meaning that is inferred or implied by a speaker in a conversation, beyond the literal or explicit meaning of the words used, relying on context and shared knowledge between the participants
19 - pragmatics and discourse analysis.coherence: the overall sense of unity, logic, and connectedness in a text or discourse, where the ideas, information, and elements are organized and presented in a clear and meaningful way
19 - pragmatics and discourse analysis.cohesion: the linguistic mechanisms used to create connections and coherence within a text by employing various cohesive devices and techniques
19 - pragmatics and discourse analysis.cohesion tie: a specific linguistic element or device that connects different parts of a text, contributing to the overall coherence and unity of the discourse
19 - pragmatics and discourse analysis.circumlocution: the use of an indirect expression to describe something
19 - pragmatics and discourse analysis.euphemism: a word or expression that is used instead of a harsh or insulting one in order to be more tactful and polite
19 - pragmatics and discourse analysis.equivocation: the deliberate use of ambiguous language or expressions to avoid making a clear or definite statement
19 - pragmatics and discourse analysis.holophrasis: (linguistics) the prelinguistic practice of expressing a whole idea in a single word
19 - pragmatics and discourse analysis.colloquialism: a word or phrase that is not formal or literary and is used in everyday conversations
19 - pragmatics and discourse analysis.malapropism: the humorous and incorrect use of a word that sounds similar to the intended word
19 - pragmatics and discourse analysis.utterance: a unit of speech or writing that is complete and coherent, usually consisting of one or more words and conveying a specific meaning or message
19 - pragmatics and discourse analysis.pleonasm: (linguistics) the redundant use of words in a way that might be considered a fault of style, or to create an emphatic effect
19 - pragmatics and discourse analysis.tmesis: (linguistics) the separation of parts of a compound word by insertion of one or more words, often in informal speech
19 - pragmatics and discourse analysis.rhetorical question: a question that is not meant to be answered, but is instead used to make a point or to create emphasis or effect
19 - pragmatics and discourse analysis.display question: a type of interrogative sentence that is asked not to obtain information but rather to make a statement or express an attitude
19 - pragmatics and discourse analysis.referential question: a type of interrogative sentence that seeks specific information or references a particular entity, object, or concept
19 - pragmatics and discourse analysis.focus: the emphasis or prominence placed on a particular element or information in a sentence or discourse
19 - pragmatics and discourse analysis.bilingual pun: a wordplay or joke that relies on the use of multiple languages, often involving the similarity or ambiguity of words or phrases in different languages to create humorous or clever effects
19 - pragmatics and discourse analysis.backchannel: the verbal and non-verbal cues, such as nodding, "uh-huh," or other short responses, that listeners use to indicate their engagement and understanding during a conversation
19 - pragmatics and discourse analysis.proverb: a well-known statement or phrase that expresses a general truth or gives advice
19 - pragmatics and discourse analysis.deictic: a word or expression that relies on the context of the utterance for its interpretation, particularly in terms of spatial, temporal, or personal reference

20 - sociolinguistics.dialect: the spoken form of a language specific to a certain region or people which is slightly different from the standard form in words and grammar
20 - sociolinguistics.accent: a manner of speaking that indicates social class, nationality, or locality of the speaker
20 - sociolinguistics.vernacular: the everyday language spoken by a particular group of people in a specific region or community
20 - sociolinguistics.standard language: a regulated and accepted form of a language that is widely used in formal settings, education, government, and media
20 - sociolinguistics.register: (linguistics) a variety of language that is used in a particular social context, based on the communicative purpose and social status of the user
20 - sociolinguistics.jargon: words, phrases, and expressions used by a specific group or profession, which are incomprehensible to others
20 - sociolinguistics.idolect: the unique language variety or style of an individual speaker
20 - sociolinguistics.free variation: the phenomenon in which multiple forms or variants of a linguistic element, such as a phoneme, morpheme, or word, can be used interchangeably without affecting the meaning or grammaticality of a sentence
20 - sociolinguistics.regional dialect: a variety of a language that is spoken in a specific geographical region
20 - sociolinguistics.social dialect: a variation of a language associated with a specific social group or class, characterized by distinct linguistic features influenced by social factors
20 - sociolinguistics.native language: the first language or mother tongue that a person acquires naturally from birth or early childhood and is typically the language they are most proficient in
20 - sociolinguistics.prestige: the social value and perceived status associated with a particular language, dialect, or speech variety
20 - sociolinguistics.received pronunciation: a prestigious and historically influential accent and pronunciation variant of standard british english, commonly associated with educated speakers in the united kingdom
20 - sociolinguistics.speech community: a group of people who share a common language or variety of a language and interact with one another using that language or variety

9 - types of board games.quad-ominos: a tile-based game where players match and place curved tiles with different numbers to create a connected network of curves and score points
9 - types of board games.go: an ancient two-player strategy board game that originated in china over 2,500 years ago

9 - types of board games.stratego: a strategy board game where two players command armies of different ranks and attempt to capture the opponent's flag while protecting their own

9 - types of board games.reversi: a strategic board game for two players who take turns placing pieces on the board, with the objective of flipping the opponent's pieces to their own color to win

9 - types of board games.mensch: a classic german board game for 2-4 players that involves rolling dice and moving pieces around the board to be the first player to move all their pieces into their respective "home" spaces
9 - types of board games.renju: a strategic board game played on a 15x15 grid, where players aim to form a row of five stones in a row while blocking their opponent from doing the same
9 - types of board games.ouija: a board game that is often used as a tool for communicating with spirits or other supernatural entities, where players rest their hands on a planchette that moves to spell out messages on the board in response to questions asked by the players

10 - board game terms.turn: the time when someone has the opportunity, obligation, or right to do a certain thing that everyone does successively in a group
10 - board game terms.capture: the act of removing an opponent's game piece from the board
10 - board game terms.move: a change made by a player in the position of a piece in a board game
10 - board game terms.staging area: a designated space on the game board where players can place their game pieces or tokens before they are put into play
10 - board game terms.custodian capture: a capture when an opponent's game piece is blocked on adjacent sides by two or more of the capturing player's pieces. the blocked piece is then removed from the game board as a result of the capture
10 - board game terms.displacement capture: a capture method used in some board games where a player's game piece is removed from the board and replaced by the capturing player's piece
10 - board game terms.doublet: a roll of two dice that show the same number
10 - board game terms.triplet: a set of three game pieces or cards or dice that share the same attributes, such as color, shape, or value
10 - board game terms.file: a vertical column of squares on a game board
10 - board game terms.gameplay: the set of activities, actions, and interactions that take place during the course of a board game or video game
10 - board game terms.grace: a bonus turn granted to a player that allows them to take an additional action or move beyond what would normally be allowed in a single turn
10 - board game terms.handicap: a set of rules or conditions that are put in place to balance the game and give a disadvantaged player a better chance of winning
10 - board game terms.huff: the ability of a player to capture an opponent's game piece by removing it from the board when the opponent fails to capture one of the player's pieces that is able to make a capture move on the same turn
10 - board game terms.in hand: used to refer to the cards, pieces, etc. that a player holds and has not yet played
10 - board game terms.intervention capture: the ability of a player to capture an opponent's game piece that has just made a capture move, by moving one of their own pieces to a square adjacent to the captured piece
10 - board game terms.pie rule: a rule used to determine who plays first in the game, and to ensure that the starting player does not have an unfair advantage over their opponent
10 - board game terms.rank: a straight line of spaces running horizontally across the gameboard at a right angle to a column
10 - board game terms.to bear off: (in backgammon) to safely bring one's pieces home and out of the game
10 - board game terms.defector: a player who switches allegiances or teams, typically to gain an advantage or for strategic reasons
10 - board game terms.boneyard: a central reserve or stockpile of unused tiles, cards, or pieces that players can draw from during the game when they need additional resources or replacements
10 - board game terms.domino toppling: a chain reaction where players set up a line of dominoes to knock one another down in a visually pleasing way

11 - tabletop game components.checkerboard: a square board that is typically used for playing the game of checkers
11 - tabletop game components.currency: a type of game component that represents a unit of value that can be exchanged for goods, services, or points
11 - tabletop game components.component: any physical element of the game, such as game pieces, cards, boards, dice, timers, or any other object that is used to play the game
11 - tabletop game components.empty board: a game board that does not have any game pieces or tokens on it at the beginning of the game
11 - tabletop game components.counter: a small usually round object included in some board games to mark a player's place or score
11 - tabletop game components.jetton: a small, round, flat piece or token used as a form of currency in various games, especially in gambling and board games
11 - tabletop game components.token: a small, physical object or symbol that represents something else, often used as a unit of value or as a marker in games or transactions
11 - tabletop game components.piece: one of the small objects that a player moves around in board games
11 - tabletop game components.peg: a small marker or token used to keep score on a scoring board or define locations etc.
11 - tabletop game components.meeple: a small, humanoid-shaped game piece used in various board games to represent a player's character or avatar on the game board
11 - tabletop game components.dice: a small cube used in games of chance with six sides each having one to six spots representing numbers
11 - tabletop game components.miniature: a small-scale representation of a character, creature, or object used in tabletop games like wargames, board games, and role-playing games to enhance visual gameplay
11 - tabletop game components.trading card: a trading card is a collectible card featuring images or information related to a specific theme, and it is often used in games or exchanged among enthusiasts
11 - tabletop game components.tile: game equipment consisting of a flat thin piece marked with characters and used in board games like mah-jong, scrabble, etc.
11 - tabletop game components.gameboard: a flat surface, typically made of cardboard, wood, or plastic, that serves as the playing area for a board game
11 - tabletop game components.spinner: a device with a pivoting arrow or pointer used to determine outcomes or actions during gameplay
11 - tabletop game components.score pad: a notepad or sheet used to record scores and keep track of points or progress in a game
11 - tabletop game components.player aid card: a reference card or cheat sheet that provides helpful information or reminders about the rules, actions, or strategies in a game, assisting players during gameplay
11 - tabletop game components.play money: fake money used in games and activities to pretend to buy and sell things without using real money
11 - tabletop game components.chip: a small, round, flat object, usually made of plastic or clay, that represents a certain amount of money or value and is used for betting and wagering
11 - tabletop game components.squidger: a tool used in the game of tiddlywinks to press down on a winkle and make it jump
11 - tabletop game components.winkle: a small, round disc made of plastic or other material, which players attempt to flip into a cup using a squidger, a larger disk-like tool
11 - tabletop game components.domino: each of a set of small flat blocks, made of wood, plastic, etc., with spots that represent numbers on one side, used in specific games
11 - tabletop game components.cribbage board: a scoring tool used in the card game cribbage, featuring a series of holes or tracks to keep track of points earned during the game

12 - types and variants of chess.shogi: a two-player strategy board game from japan, similar to chess, where players move pieces with different abilities across a board to capture their opponent's pieces and ultimately checkmate their opponent's king
12 - types and variants of chess.janggi: a two-player strategy board game from korea, similar to xiangqi and shogi, where players move pieces with different abilities across a board to capture their opponent's pieces and ultimately checkmate their opponent's king

12 - types and variants of chess.racing kings: a chess variant where both players race their king to the eighth rank to win the game

12 - types and variants of chess.crazyhouse chess: a chess variant where captured pieces can be reintroduced into play as one's own
12 - types and variants of chess.three-check chess: a chess variant where the objective is to give the opponent's king three checks, instead of checkmate, to win the game
12 - types and variants of chess.blitz chess: a variant of chess with faster time controls, where players have limited time to make their moves, typically ranging from a few minutes to a few seconds per move
12 - types and variants of chess.makruk: a two-player strategy board game from thailand, similar to chess, where players move pieces with different abilities across a board to capture their opponent's pieces and ultimately checkmate their opponent's king

12 - types and variants of chess.circular chess: a variant of the traditional chess game played on a circular board with unique movement patterns for some pieces
12 - types and variants of chess.gothic chess: a chess variant that introduces new pieces and changes the initial setup of the traditional chess game
12 - types and variants of chess.atomic chess: a chess variant where capturing a piece causes an "explosion," removing the capturing piece and all adjacent pieces from the board
